raw_response:
Alright, let me think through this year like I always do, field by field.

---

This year's the same as most years — I've got my 8 mu, and I split it the way we always do: the 5 mu near the road stays in wheat-maize, the other 3 mu at the back is cotton land. That land has been cotton for a long time, no use changing.

**Wheat.** The wheat's already in the ground — I put it down last October like everybody. I used seed I kept back from last year's harvest, saves money. Before planting I spread one bag of that compound fertilizer with the three numbers on it — one bag per mu, that's what my mother-in-law always did and it works fine. Now it's spring and the wheat is greening up. In a week or two when it starts jointing I'll spread half a bag of urea per mu. If it looks a bit yellow I'll do a little more, but I can't waste it. I'll need to pump water from the well — once for green-up, once at jointing, and one more at grain-filling if the rains don't come. Pumping costs diesel so I don't do it unless the leaves start rolling. Harvest in June — we hire the combine man from the village, costs money but there's no other way, the work has to get done in three or four days before the maize needs planting.

**Maize.** Right after we cut the wheat — maybe five days, no more — we have to plant maize or we lose yield. I buy hybrid seed from the shop in town, you can't save it, it doesn't come back true. I'll put some compound fertilizer at planting and topdress urea once when the corn is about knee-high. If rain comes I don't irrigate, but usually we pump once in July if it's dry. Spray herbicide early, that's all. Maize is easier than cotton, less worry.

**Cotton.** The 3 mu of cotton — I plant in late April, when the ground is warm. I buy cotton seed each year, the improved kind everyone uses. Cotton takes the most work. I put one bag of compound at planting, then topdress urea when it's flowering. The hard part is the bugs — the bollworm will eat everything if you don't watch. I spray maybe four or five times through the summer. My neighbor sprays more but I can't afford it. Picking starts in September and goes to October, three or four passes through the field. My mother-in-law helps me pick, and my older daughter on weekends when she's not in school. If it's a heavy year I call my sister to come help for a week.

**About the money.** My husband works in the town most of the year, sends money back. I have to be careful — the kids' school things, food, and then seeds and fertilizer and the well and the diesel. I don't spend more than I have. If the cotton price is good we do well, if not we get by on the maize and the wheat flour we keep for the family.
